source.title: Incomplete Prompt Jailbreaks in Large Language Models
source.authors: Y. Kim; Bumjin Park; Jaesik Choi

record.tranche_reason: The study uses selected neurons as a tool for steering jailbreak responses and reports steering outcomes. It does not test the listed claims about neuron-pole interpretability, explanation validity, or attribution graphs.
record.gate_note: The neuron-steering results are recorded as findings about neuron-level intervention, but they do not measure any listed version. The paper does not audit neuron poles, test explanations on held-out activations, or build attribution graphs. Other jailbreak-rate results and cited findings do not test the listed neuron claims.
record.test_reason: The study selects MLP neurons by correlation with termination tokens or by instruction-contrast set differences, then steers them to change refusal and harmful-output rates in jailbreak settings. It never audits how many neurons have one main job, scores neuron explanations, examines canonical polysemantic neurons, or builds attribution graphs. Its neuron results concern steering effects on jailbreak behaviour, not neuron interpretability shares or explanation validity.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that incomplete prompts raise attack success over complete prompts across models, and that refusals appear mainly after sentence termination. They further conclude that LoRA abrupt-refusal tuning fails to generalize across content, attractors and refusal styles, while neuron-level control is a promising finer-grained defense. They acknowledge that precise causal neuron mechanisms are not established.
record.recipe_differences: This study identifies neuron sets through termination-token correlations or instruction contrasts and steers their activations to affect jailbreak responses. It does not use the original sources' neuron-explanation audit or attribution-graph procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering strength changes the reported outcomes; excessive termination-neuron steering reduces refusals and can produce unrelated content. The study also reports different effects for termination, NonTerm–JailTerm, and JailTerm–NonTerm neuron sets.

fits_no_version.finding: Termination-correlated neurons raise immediate refusals at strength 2.0 but produce unrelated content at 4.0. The NonTerm–JailTerm set raises harmful outputs, and JailTerm–NonTerm gives only a limited refusal increase.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small sets of MLP neurons selected by termination-token correlation or instruction contrast causally modulate refusal and harmful continuation, with effects depending on steering strength.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering a single anti-termination neuron on XSTest trades unsafe refusal against benign utility across strengths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single steered neuron can broadly suppress refusal behaviour, producing a safety–utility tradeoff.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper states that it does not provide a detailed framework linking inputs, functional neurons, and control signals, limiting precise neuron-level causal claims. Several steering results are presented in figures without numeric values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: General task benchmark results in Table 9 were not included because they report capability effects of steering rather than a result on any listed neuron-interpretability claim.

Whether activating-example explanations predict neuron firing.

record.verdict_notes: This is a jailbreak and safety paper that uses neurons only as steering handles. Table 10's neuron counts per layer are selection values, not interpretability results. Not an original source.
